strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP safety problem through a broad comparison of 13 jailbreak methods, six models, and 16 violation categories. Its consolidation of attack families and evaluation settings has practical value.

Human validation of the automated judge is a substantive strength: 640 responses receive three annotations, with Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and reported judge–human agreement of 94.84%. These results provide useful evidence of annotation consistency.

No-attack baselines, three experimental repetitions, detailed model/category breakdowns, and transfer and runtime analyses make the empirical findings inspectable. The strong performance of simple human-written prompts is particularly useful for informing baseline selection.
weaknesses: Attack budgets and success measures are not sufficiently comparable. Sections 5.3–5.4 score Generation Exploitation as successful if any of 50 responses succeeds, while describing other methods as top-1 evaluation. Counting prompt modifications also does not equalize target queries or computational cost. A fixed-decoding repeated-sampling baseline and success-versus-budget comparisons are needed to substantiate the claimed effectiveness and efficiency advantages.

The success criterion does not fully establish successful harmful assistance. Section 5.3 describes Label C as checking correctness, but Figure 9 checks direct or indirect relatedness; Label B also accepts willingness. The rule combining A/B/C into final success is unspecified. Aggregate human agreement is encouraging, but clearer request-fulfillment criteria and targeted error analysis are needed to establish what the reported ASRs measure.

The policy-compliance interpretation needs question-level validation. Categories such as AI disclosure and professional advice involve deployment context, so an on-topic response does not necessarily establish a violation. Moreover, Table 3 reports baseline ASRs of 0.84 for Political Activities and 0.93 for AI Usage Disclosure, exceeding attack averages of 0.71 and 0.68. Reporting success on initially refused questions would help distinguish existing behavior from safeguards actually bypassed.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the proposed benchmark. The manuscript supplies neither the complete 160-question dataset nor a repository, omits the judge’s few-shot demonstrations, and leaves important details unspecified, including dated API versions and the 50 decoding configurations. GCG uses 500 steps in Sections 5.4 and 7.1 but 50 in Table 8. These omissions and inconsistencies prevent independent reproduction of central results.

Baseline fidelity is uncertain. Section 3.3 substitutes rewriting the AIM template for Masterkey because its code was unavailable, without demonstrating that this reproduces the described learned attack. Results for this proxy cannot confidently support conclusions about Masterkey itself.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. AutoDAN and Generation Exploitation averages cover three open models, whereas most methods are averaged across six; these averages cannot directly establish overall superiority. AIM also achieves the highest ASR on four targets, qualifying the claim that optimized prompts consistently perform best. Ten questions per category and transfer from only Vicuna further limit broad generalization.
